targetReport.title: Valuation of Land Act 1960 (Vic)
targetReport.description: The Victorian analog to NSW's Valuation of Land Act 1916: establishes the office of Valuer-General (Part I) and requires an annual general valuation of rateable land statewide. Section 11 (as substituted by No. 69/2011 s.53): a valuation authority must 'cause a general valuation of rateable land within an area to be made as at 1 January in each calendar year' and, 'before 30 April that year,' cause it to be returned and provided to the relevant council. VERIFIED DIRECTLY: the official source (legislation.vic.gov.au) is a JS-rendered SPA whose raw HTML doesn't yield section text via regex, and the AustLII mirror is Cloudflare-blocked in this environment; full consolidated text instead fetched and confirmed via a third-party legal mirror, the FAO Legal Office's legislation database (faolex.fao.org), then extracted with pdftotext.
targetReport.cadence_note: Section 11 mandates a genuinely annual valuation cycle (valuation date 1 January, return due before 30 April each calendar year) -- unlike NSW, where the Valuation of Land Act 1916 requires annual ascertainment in principle but current council practice runs on an operational three-year cycle. Victoria's own valuations-process page confirms the Valuer-General has been the single valuation authority for all 79 Victorian councils since 2023.

release_schedule.note: The Valuation of Land Act 1960 (Vic) is a piece of Victorian legislation, not a recurring statistical/administrative publication. Victoria's official legislation register (legislation.vic.gov.au) shows a version-history/reprint page with 70+ consolidated versions dating back to 1997, with new versions issued whenever amending Acts or statutory rules take effect (e.g. 4 Dec 2024, 1 Jan 2025, 1 Jul 2025 - three updates within about seven months). There is no fixed cadence, calendar, or stated rule governing when the next amendment/reprint will occur; it is amended irregularly by the Victorian Parliament as needed. This is a foundational legal instrument, not a true recurring release.

results.window: Este tipo de trabajo no se cuantifica en el marco central de la contabilidad nacional.Para la elaboración de la CSTNRHM se requirieron datos sobre el TNRH, así como de la información sobre elcosto al que ha de valorarse ese tiempo.Principales fuentes deinformaciónLa fuente principal para determinar el tiempo destinado al TNRH es la Encuesta Nacional de Uso del Tiempo(ENUT), la cual permite conocer a la población que realiza estos trabajos y las horas que le destinan. Para elcaso de la población de entre 5 y 11 años, las fuentes principales son el Módulo de Trabajo Infantil (MTI) queofrece la Encuesta Nacional de Ocupación y Empleo (ENOE) y la Encuesta Nacional de Trabajo Infantil (ENTI).En los años que no se dispuso de información de las fuentes principales, se utilizó la Encuesta Nacional deEmpleo (ENE); la ENOE y su transición a la ENOE, nueva edición, (ENOEN), así como la Encuesta Telefónicade Ocupación y Empleo (ETOE).Para determinar el costo por hora al que se valora el tiempo de TNRH, se utilizó la información de la ENE,ENOE, ENOEN y ETOE en materia de ingresos por hora en cifras netas por ocupación. Para proporcionar losvalores en cifras brutas, se recurrió a los datos de las remuneraciones medias por actividad económica delSistema de Cuentas Nacionales de México (SCNM).Los clasificadores que se emplearon para identificar las actividades económicas, así como las ocupacionesque son objeto de estudio de la CSTNRHM, fueron los siguientes: la Clasificación Mexicana de Actividadesde Uso del Tiempo, el Sistema de Clasificación Industrial de América del Norte (SCIAN) 2018, la ClasificaciónMexicana de Ocupaciones y el Sistema Nacional de Clasificación de Ocupaciones (SINCO).Nota a las personasusuariasLa CSTNRHM 2024, preliminar, incorpora los resultados de la ENUT 2024, con lo que se obtuvo una serie detiempo con diferencias respecto a la versión 2023 preliminar.Adicionalmente, estos resultados se encuentran alineados con la ENUT, ediciones 2014 y 2019, y la ENOE,del primer trimestre de 2005 al cuarto de 2024, cuyas estimaciones de población se actualizaron con baseen el marco muestral del Censo de Población y Vivienda (CPV) 2020.

results.basis: Catalogue 15F0077GIE, 'A Guide to Deflating the Input-Output Accounts: Sources and Methods' (2001), which record 1301 cites as the description of the double-deflation method used to produce constant-price GDP by industry. Under the heading 'Sources of deflators', unhedged: 'The main data source of deflators for manufactured goods is the Industrial Product Price Indexes (IPPI) produced by Statistics Canada's Prices Division. Prior to 1981, deflators were based on Industry Selling Price Indexes (ISPI).' Earlier in the same chapter, on why basic-price deflation is possible where purchaser-price deflation is not: 'the commodity price information collected by the Prices Division to compile industry product price indexes can be used to construct deflators for values at basic prices. These Industrial Product Price Indexes (IPPI), aggregated where necessary to the input-output classification, constitute the main source of deflators for manufactured commodities.' Both passages verified verbatim against the PDF. `methodology_depends_on` matches the type taken for statcan-sut -> statcan-cpi from the same document. ONE HEDGE, STATED, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE: the guide is a 2001 edition marked ARCHIVED, twenty-five years old, and it remains the document record 1301 points at for this method. The 'can be used' softness that qualifies the CPI edge does not apply here — the 'Sources of deflators' sentence says 'is'.

targetReport.title: Industrial Product Price Index (IPPI)
targetReport.description: Monthly measure of price change for major commodities sold by manufacturers operating in Canada, record 2318, produced by the Prices Division alongside the Consumer Price Index. Prices are collected at the factory gate, so they are what the producer receives rather than what a purchaser pays: record 2318 states they 'exclude all indirect taxes, such as sales taxes, customs duties and tariffs as this money does not go to the factors of production', and exclude common-carrier transport and retail or wholesale distribution beyond the gate. That is the whole reason the accounts need it as well as the CPI — the supply and use tables are built at basic prices, and the CPI measures purchasers' prices. The IPPI is the deflator the Canadian accounts actually run on: it is named in 64 rows of the monthly GDP by industry source table against the CPI's 27, and the input-output deflation guide calls it 'the main data source of deflators for manufactured goods'. Record 2318 states the role in its own words: 'the IPPI series supports the Canadian System of Macro-Economic Accounts (CSMA), where it is used in the calculation of real Gross Domestic Product (GDP).' It replaced the Industry Selling Price Index in the early 1980s.
targetReport.cadence_note: Monthly, reference period month. Two lags worth knowing before this node is used for timing. Collection: 'For most products included in the IPPI, the collection process occurs over a three-week period starting during the third week of the reference month.' Revision: 'price indexes remain subject to revision for six months after publication of a given month's data', so any dependent reading a recent month is reading a provisional number. The weighting structure moves on a far slower clock than the index — 'The entire weighting scheme for the IPPI is generally revised every 5 years' — which is what the reference period on the edge to the supply and use tables records.

targetReport.title: Canada Health Transfer
targetReport.description: The largest major federal transfer to provinces and territories, providing federal cash support for health care and backing the criteria of the Canada Health Act. Finance Canada publishes provincial and territorial entitlement amounts each year before the start of the fiscal year.
